article: 加速度センサーの仕組み
findings: Clarified that an accelerometer responds to specific force: a supported stationary device reads about 1g, while ideal free fall is near 0g.

Added the limitation that accelerometer-only data cannot separate gravity from linear acceleration; tilt estimation assumes gravity is the dominant stimulus, and fusion algorithms may use gyroscope data.

Replaced the oversimplified claim that capacitance always changes inversely with electrode gap; the ideal parallel-plate equation is shown with a note that MEMS geometries can change gap or overlap area.
Qualified piezoresistive and automotive crash-sensing examples; clarified that airbag deployment is determined by a validated vehicle control system.
Removed unsupported historical and size claims and restored the single original publication date 2026-10-01.

meaning.note: Compared the full localized article with the Japanese source: specific-force interpretation, supported rest versus free fall, gravity-based tilt assumptions, proof-mass displacement, both sensing methods, application limits, and the references.

terminology.note: Checked localized terminology for acceleration, specific force, proof mass, MEMS, damping, capacitance, permittivity, piezoresistive sensing, bridge circuit, gyroscope, and sensor fusion.

mathematics.note: Checked F=ma, standard gravity g0=9.80665 m/s^2, the near-1g supported-rest and near-0g free-fall examples, and the ideal parallel-plate capacitance equation C=epsilon A/d. Clarified that motion and gravity cannot be separated by an accelerometer alone.

code.note: The article contains no executable code or software instructions.

links.note: Checked six manufacturer/application sources from STMicroelectronics, Analog Devices, Bosch Sensortec, and PCB Piezotronics for MEMS structure, tilt assumptions, sensor fusion, capacitive sensing, automotive crash sensing, and high-shock piezoresistive sensors.
